videos.title: Three Parts and a Bus
videos.opensFrom: The start of the course: nothing installed but Tuner X.
videos.handsTo: 'Red means two devices share an ID' hands to Motor Setup; the name canivore is what the code matches in Mechanisms.
videos.gate: None. A procedure, recorded.
videos.visuals: Animated: laptop → USB → CANivore → devices, a greyed 'robot controller' the packet skips. Recorded: CANivore USB, localhost, rename (staged), batch firmware, power cycle. Card colours as a still strip (only green can be shown live).
lines: Every mechanism in this workshop is three parts: a motor, a sensor, and a bus that connects them to your laptop.
The motor has its controller built into the back. It runs its own control loop and reports its own position, so the motor is a sensor too.
The arm also gets an absolute encoder. It still knows the arm's angle after the power's been off all week. The flywheel doesn't need one.
The CANivore gives those devices their own bus, and your laptop plugs straight into it. There's no robot in between, so you can start right now.
Power the mechanism first, then plug in the USB. In Tuner X, turn on CANivore USB, and set the address to localhost.
Your CANivore shows up. Rename it canivore, all lowercase. Every line of code in this course uses that name, so spell it exactly the same.
Old firmware still connects, and then it fails later in ways that come and go. Put every device on the same version.
The card's color tells you where you stand. Green is current. Yellow means there's an update. Red means two devices share an ID, and that's the next lesson.
Power cycle everything. The name and the firmware live on the devices, so they come back exactly as you left them.
Three parts, one bus, and a name that matches the code.

videos.title: Numbers and First Motion
videos.opensFrom: Last video's red card: two devices sharing an ID.
videos.handsTo: Voltage Out 'pushed the moment you enabled it' and 'kept running until you stopped it' are what Java Basics and the Latched Request call back to.
videos.gate: Animated insert: the arm at 1 V with no target; the student enables and must stop it before the end of travel.
videos.visuals: Recorded: three dots → Factory Default, Blink with a camera inset of the LEDs, IDs 31/32/21, CANcoder hand test and zero (needs the arm build), Feedback section, Control → Voltage Out at 1 V, Disabled/Enabled. Animated: the no-target sweep and the Disable button.
lines: Before anything moves, every device gets its own number.
Open the motor, and factory default it. That clears whatever last season left behind.
Click Blink. The device that flashes is the one you're editing. If two flash together, they share an ID.
Give each one its number and a name. The arm's motor is thirty one, its encoder is thirty two, and the flywheel is twenty one.
On the arm, turn it counterclockwise by hand, and the encoder's number should climb. Zero it with the arm level, and a quarter turn up reads point two five.
Then tell the arm's motor to use that encoder for its position. In the feedback settings, that's the encoder's ID, and remote CANcoder.
Now the first motion. Pick Voltage Out, and ask for one volt. It sends that voltage and nothing else. There's no target, and no place to stop.
Enable it. The mechanism moves the moment you click, and it keeps going until you click again.
Try it. Enable it, and stop it before it reaches the end.
Check the direction. The arm should turn counterclockwise, with the encoder counting up. If it goes the wrong way, invert the motor in its settings. Don't type a negative voltage.
Every device has its own number, and positive means the same thing everywhere, before any code runs.

videos.title: One Motion, Then Silence
videos.opensFrom: Voltage Out had no target; now the motor gets one.
videos.handsTo: The three shapes (runs away, buzzes, falls short) are called back by Drive to Point and Profiled Drive to Point. Hands off to the page's MechanismPlayground rather than duplicating it.
videos.gate: Pick a kP that's too low, then too high, and read the plot. Mirrors the playground; the video's version is three fixed choices.
videos.visuals: Animated: gravity arrow shrinking with cos(angle) and the kG counter-arrow matching it; the three kP shapes as arm + trace, then the arm stripped away; a stacked output bar (feedforward slab, feedback sliver). Recorded: plot setup, Slot 0 to zero, enable on zero gains, kG/kP/kD steps with every value masked, apply and power cycle.
lines: The motor runs its own control loop. Tuner X just sends it a target, and draws what happens.
Start with every gain at zero, and enable. Nothing moves. That's correct: zero gains mean zero volts.
Gravity pulls hardest when the arm is level, and not at all when it's straight up.
The gravity gain cancels exactly that pull, at every angle. Raise it until the arm holds level on its own.
The static gain covers friction. Set it to half the gap between the smallest and largest gravity gains that hold.
Now the feedback. Double the proportional gain until the arm overshoots, then cut it in half.
The derivative gain takes out the overshoot. Too much of it, and the arm buzzes.
Try it. Pick a gain that's too low, then one that's too high, and watch the plot.
Three shapes tell you what's wrong. It runs away, it buzzes, or it falls short. Read the plot, not the mechanism.
Apply the gains, and power cycle. They're saved on the motor.
Feedforward pays for holding. Feedback fixes what's left. A tuned arm makes one motion, and then it's silent.

videos.title: Walking the Target
videos.opensFrom: Last video's target jumped all at once.
videos.handsTo: Owns the trapezoid ('speed up, cruise, slow down'), which Naming a Target and Profiled Drive to Point call back to. Ends on Generate Code, where Configs and Requests picks up.
videos.gate: Shorten the move and watch the cruise disappear: the triangle.
videos.visuals: Animated: three synced panels on one playhead (ghost setpoint arm, velocity trapezoid, position S-curve); the triangle on a short move; flywheel with cruise greyed 'not read'. Recorded: Motion Magic config (cruise 0.5, accel 1, jerk 0), Control → MotionMagicVoltage at 0.25, the plot's ramp-cruise-ramp, raising limits, three dots → Generate Code. Slot 0 values masked.
lines: Last time, the target jumped all at once. Motion Magic walks it there instead.
Two numbers describe the walk: how fast it may go, and how fast it may speed up.
So every move has three parts. It speeds up, it cruises, and it slows down, arriving with no speed left.
Your gains don't change. Motion Magic only moves the target they chase.
In the Motion Magic settings, start slow: half a rotation per second, and one rotation per second squared. Leave jerk at zero, and apply.
Pick Motion Magic from the control menu, ask for a quarter turn, and enable. The plot draws the shape.
Try it. Make the move shorter, and watch what happens to the cruise.
On a short move, there's no room to cruise. It starts slowing down before it reaches top speed, and that's correct.
A flywheel isn't going anywhere, so it has no cruise. Only the acceleration shapes its ramp.
Raise the limits one step at a time, until the arm starts to lag, then back off a little.
Everything you set now lives on the motor. In the three dot menu, Generate Code copies it out, and that's where the code picks up in Workshop 3.
Name where it should end up, and the motor plans the way there.

videos.title: Handing Over Code
videos.opensFrom: Tuner X: Voltage Out pushed the instant you enabled it.
videos.handsTo: Names the 'someone' who runs the command: the scheduler.
videos.gate: Two keys: C calls the method (a sealed package lands in a command, arm stays still), S runs the command (package opens every loop, arm moves).
videos.visuals: runSlow() code; a sealed 'package' token holding setVoltage(3.0); a command card; loop pulse; TalonFX card; arm. No controller yet.
lines: Most of the Java in this course is ordinary: classes, fields, methods. One piece works differently, and everything else is built on it.
In Tuner X, the motor pushed the moment you enabled Voltage Out. Code doesn't have to work that way.
Here's a method on the arm. It builds a command that pushes the arm at three volts.
That little arrow makes a lambda. It turns the code after it into a package that's written down and handed over, but not run.
So when this method runs, the motor doesn't move. You get back a command with that package inside, and that's all.
There's no error and no warning. The arm just sits there, because nothing has run the command yet.
When something does run it, the package opens, and it keeps opening every loop. Now the motor gets its three volts.
Try it. Call the method, then run the command, and watch which one moves the arm.
A lambda is code you hand to something else to run later. Next, you'll meet what runs it.

videos.title: The Scheduler
videos.opensFrom: Last video's package needed something to run it.
videos.handsTo: Lanes and owners are reused by every later video; the empty lane before the first press is left unexplained on purpose (latched owns it).
videos.gate: Hold either trigger or both; each mechanism's lane changes owner independently.
videos.visuals: When/What/How cards; a 50-per-second tick clock; one lane per mechanism (Arm, Flywheel) with command blocks; controller with both triggers; Robot.robotPeriodic and the MyTeleop bindings; flywheel drawable (new).
lines: Robot code comes down to three things. Triggers say when. Mechanisms are what moves. Commands say how.
Last time, a command was a package waiting for something to run it. That something is the scheduler.
Fifty times a second, the robot calls one line, and the scheduler takes a turn. It checks every trigger, starts and cancels commands, and runs whatever's scheduled.
Each mechanism gets a lane, and a lane holds one command at a time.
Hold the left trigger. The command that pushes at six volts takes the arm's lane. It owns the arm now, and nothing else can drive that motor.
That command never decides to stop on its own. Ending it is the trigger's job.
Let go, and in a single tick it's canceled, and the stop command takes the lane.
Your turn. Hold one trigger, then both. Each mechanism has its own lane, so each one has its own owner.
If a second command asks for a lane that's already taken, the newcomer wins, and the old one is canceled.
Fifty times a second, the scheduler decides which one command owns each mechanism.

videos.title: Configs and Requests
videos.opensFrom: Tuner X Generate Code: the config you built by hand gets pasted here.
videos.handsTo: Plants 'the last request sticks', which the latched video pays off. Ends on Robot owning the arm once, which OpModes uses.
videos.gate: Drag the arm to any angle, press power. The motor's own count snaps to zero; the CANcoder keeps the real angle.
videos.visuals: Arm.java (fields, pasted config, two private methods); TalonFX card split into Config (stays) and Current request (changes); CAN wire with a one-shot config packet and repeating request packets; CANcoder with absolute angle beside the rotor count; power button with a blackout; Robot.java fields. Folds in /project-structure's one animated idea (Robot builds the mechanisms once).
lines: A mechanism is one part of the robot, written as one class. This one's the arm.
In Tuner X, you set this motor up by hand. Generate Code copies those settings out. That copy goes right here, in the constructor.
First, the hardware: the CAN bus, the motor on thirty one, and the CANcoder on thirty two.
When the arm gets built, the constructor sends that config to the motor once. The motor saves it and keeps it.
A request is different. It says what to do right now, and the code sends a new one every loop.
Whichever request arrives last is the one the motor keeps doing. Hold on to that. It comes back in a few lessons.
One setting matters more than it looks. The motor counts its own turns, but that count starts over at zero every time the robot powers on.
Try it. Move the arm, power cycle the robot, and compare the two readings.
The CANcoder remembers the real angle. These lines make it the motor's source, so every angle you ask for later is a real one.
Last, the robot builds the arm once, as a field, and every mode you write uses that same arm.
Settings go in once. Requests go every loop, and the last one sticks.

videos.title: Every Command Is a Hold
videos.opensFrom: The setters were made private in Mechanisms; the package arrow from Java Basics.
videos.handsTo: Ends on the question 'what ends a hold?', which OpModes answers.
videos.gate: Three chips (three volts, six volts, stop). Tap one, watch its request land every loop; tap another, watch it take over.
videos.visuals: Lock on setVoltage; Arm.java commands typing in; a builder piece that snaps into a command when .named attaches; loop pulse; TalonFX card; owner badge on the arm.
lines: The arm's setters are private, so nothing outside the arm can call them. A command is the only way in.
Here's the first one. It pushes at three volts.
You've seen the arrow before. It hands the job over, and this part runs that job every loop, for as long as the command runs.
The name on the end is what makes it a command. Leave it off, and the build fails with an error that doesn't tell you why.
The other two work the same way: six volts, and stop. Even stop sends its zero every loop.
Try it. Pick a command and watch the request it sends, then pick another.
Look at the word at the end of every name. Hold. None of these ever finishes. Each one runs until something else takes the arm.
So what takes it? On the robot, it's the driver's thumb, and that's the next lesson.

videos.title: Two Edges
videos.opensFrom: A hold never ends on its own (last video).
videos.handsTo: 'Every hold needs a release' sets up the latched video, which removes one.
videos.gate: Right trigger held, flywheel spinning. Pick what the release runs (stop, three volts, six volts), then let go.
videos.visuals: Generated MyTeleop collapsing into three bindings; driver station mode list (Teleop / My Auto) with a ghost second Teleop struck off; press/release edge strip under the controller; flywheel and arm; lanes from The Scheduler.
lines: An OpMode is one way the robot can run. Teleop is one of them, and each one is its own class.
The project creator already made a teleop for you. The annotation at the top is what puts it on the driver station.
So edit that file. Don't add a second one, or you'll end up with two teleops on the list.
Clear out the empty methods, and bind the buttons in the constructor. The robot hands it the arm and the flywheel.
Every button has two edges. Pressing it is one, letting go is the other, and each edge gets its own binding.
Hold the left trigger, and the arm pushes. Let go, and the release runs stop.
The right trigger's release is different. It drops the flywheel back to three volts, not to zero.
Your turn. Choose what the release does, then let go.
Bindings belong to their mode. Switch to auto, and the triggers do nothing. Switch back, and they're there again. There's nothing to clean up.
Every hold needs a release. Next, you'll see exactly what happens without one.

videos.title: The Latched Request
videos.opensFrom: Tuner X Voltage Out kept running until you stopped it.
videos.handsTo: Motion Magic in Code reverses it.
videos.gate: Hold the trigger, let go, watch it keep spinning, press Disable.
videos.visuals: Already built: lessons/latched.
lines: Built and approved. Optional tweak for continuity: open with 'Last time, every hold got a release. Let's take one away.' before the Tuner X recap.

videos.title: Naming a Target
videos.opensFrom: The latched request: last time, staying was the problem.
videos.handsTo: Commands that name a target and hold forever: Workshop 4 has to give them endings.
videos.gate: Hold the trigger and let go halfway through the move. The command ends; the arm still finishes and holds.
videos.visuals: Field swap VoltageOut to MotionMagicVoltage; Slot 0 strip at 0.0, then 'your gains' hatched (never numbers); target marker at vertical; ghost setpoint arm leading the real one; velocity-time trapezoid with a playhead; TalonFX card with a target instead of volts; a small freeze-frame of the latched runaway for contrast.
lines: A request can name a voltage, or it can name a target.
In Tuner X, you picked Motion Magic, gave it a position, and watched the arm speed up, cruise, and slow down into place.
In code, it's the same swap. The voltage request comes out, and a Motion Magic request goes in.
Your gains come from the bench. Out of the box every one of them is zero, so paste your config from Tuner X again.
The commands change too. Instead of a voltage, this one names a place: straight up.
And the release binding comes out. You'll see why in a second.
Hold the trigger. The motor plans the whole move, then follows it: speed up, cruise, slow down, arrive.
Now let go. The command ends, and the request stays on the motor, just like last time.
But this time the request is a position, so staying is exactly what holds the arm up.
Try letting go halfway through the move.
It still finishes. The motor already knows where the arm is supposed to end up.
If the arm doesn't move at all, the gains are still zero. If it overshoots and hunts, retune in Tuner X and paste again. Don't fix it in code.
Name where the arm should be, and the motor keeps it there, even after the command ends.

videos.title: Steps
videos.opensFrom: Every command so far is a hold that runs until you let go.
videos.handsTo: A one-second timeout is a guess; Finish Conditions replaces it with the sensor.
videos.gate: Remove the timeout chip from the first command and press Y again. The flywheel never starts.
videos.visuals: Introduces the scheduler timeline used for all of Workshop 4: lanes per mechanism, bars that end vs bars with no right edge, a playhead, a bracket for the group, a stopwatch chip for withTimeout. Arm stays up after its step (latched position).
lines: A routine is a list of commands that run in order.
Every command you've written so far is a hold. Hold the button, and it runs until you let go. On this timeline, that's a bar with no end.
Put a hold first in a list, and the list never moves on. There's no error. It just looks frozen.
So give it an ending. A one second timeout turns the hold into a step.
Now the list works. The arm goes up, and one second later the flywheel starts.
When the arm's step ends, the arm stays up. Its position request is still on the motor.
The flywheel is still a hold, so the whole routine is a hold too. Letting go of the button is what ends it.
Try it. Take the timeout off, and run it again.
The flywheel never starts. The list is still waiting on a command that never ends.
A race is the other way to combine commands. They run side by side, and the race ends when the first one finishes. So a hold can never win one.
Give every step an ending. The last one decides whether the whole list ends.

videos.title: Ask Every Loop
videos.opensFrom: Last video's one-second timeout was a guess.
videos.handsTo: 'A timeout is not arrival' is what Coroutines checks for with timedOut().
videos.gate: Drag the tolerance down to 0.001 degrees and run it. The stopwatch wins at two seconds; the next step starts with the arm short.
videos.visuals: Arm angle gauge with a target tick and a shaded tolerance band; the condition line pulsing each loop with a true/false chip; on the timeline, the step drawn as a race between a condition bar and a stopwatch bar.
lines: A finish condition ends a step when the mechanism says it got there.
Last time, the arm's step ended after one second. That number was a guess.
This method asks the sensor whether the arm is close enough to its target. Close enough, because a real arm is never exactly on the number.
The arrow matters again. It hands the question over, so it gets asked every loop, and the step ends on the loop the answer turns true.
Back it with a timeout. Now the step has two ways to end: the arm arrives, or the clock runs out.
On most runs, the sensor wins in about half a second.
Try it. Squeeze the tolerance down to almost nothing, and run it again.
The arm gets close, but never close enough, so the clock wins at two seconds.
And the next step starts anyway, with the arm short of its target. A timeout tells you the waiting is over. It doesn't tell you where the arm is.
End on the sensor, back it with a timer, and never treat the timer running out as arriving.

videos.title: Fork and Wait
videos.opensFrom: Autonomous: nobody is holding a button, so nobody can let go.
videos.handsTo: The routine gives up silently after three seconds, which is Logging's cold open.
videos.gate: Line one is a two-way chip: fork or await. Await freezes on line one while the 15 second auto clock drains; fork carries on.
videos.visuals: Matches the existing CoroutineTimeline component on /coroutines: main flow column, peel-off lanes for Arm and Flywheel, solid = running, dashed = waiting, two exits from a wait (arrived / gave up), a 15 s autonomous clock, driver station auto picker showing 'Raise And Shoot'. Controller idle on purpose.
lines: A coroutine is a routine written as plain code, one line after another, that can pause on a line.
In autonomous, nobody's holding a button. There's nobody to let go.
And the arm has to keep holding while everything after it happens. A list can't do that.
Fork starts a command and moves straight on. The arm's lane keeps running on its own.
Then the routine waits until the arm is in place, but never longer than three seconds.
Your turn. Fork the arm, or await it. Pick one, and run it.
Await waits for the command to finish. The arm holds forever, so the routine never gets past the first line.
If that wait runs out, the routine checks, and leaves. Without the check, it would shoot at an angle nobody looked at.
Then the flywheel spins up, the routine waits for it to reach speed, and the shot gets one second.
Last, it forks a stop for the flywheel. Ending a routine cancels everything it started, and canceling doesn't stop a motor.
Fork the holds, await the steps, put a limit on every wait, and stop what you started before you leave.

videos.title: What Nobody Watched
videos.opensFrom: Cold open: the coroutine routine gives up after three seconds and nobody sees it.
videos.handsTo: Testing: catching a problem before the robot ever runs.
videos.gate: Scrub the finished plot. Find where the routine gave up; snapping there lights the timedOut() line.
videos.visuals: Values leaving a trail on a scrolling strip that becomes a plot; enabled band and mode label; Robot constructor lines; record() with unit words glowing; the command-vs-addPeriodic replay where the trace goes flat at release. AdvantageScope itself is a short screen recording, not animated.
lines: Autonomous runs. The arm rises, stops short, and the flywheel never spins. Then it's over.
Nobody saw why. A log is a recording of numbers over time, kept in a file you can open afterwards.
Two lines in the robot's constructor start the recorder. It notes when the robot is enabled, and which mode is running.
Then the arm records three numbers: where it is, where it's trying to be, and the voltage it's using. The units go in the names.
This line runs that recording every loop, for the whole program.
Put it inside a command instead, and it only records while that command runs. Let go of the trigger, and the line goes flat even though the arm keeps moving.
Now find the moment the routine gave up.
Three seconds after the target changed, the arm was still short. That's the timeout. And the voltage was working the whole time, so this is a tuning problem, not a wiring one.
Log from the start, all the time, and the file will tell you what nobody watched.

videos.title: One Tick by Hand
videos.opensFrom: Hook: a teammate changes one number while the robot is packed in a crate.
videos.handsTo: End of the mechanism chain; Workshop 5 starts swerve.
videos.gate: Be the teammate: drag the flywheel tolerance from 0.5 up to 10 and press Run Tests. Past about 5, the second check fails.
videos.visuals: ArmTest code; a 'waiting' slot vs 'running' slot for the scheduled command; one manual tick pulse; TalonFX card reading the target; flywheel speed dial with a tolerance band and two markers (just inside, well outside); a stylised test-results panel (PASSED / FAILED with a line number).
lines: Three weeks before an event, a teammate changes one number. The robot's packed in a crate. Who notices?
A test is a check the computer runs for you, every time the code changes.
Hardware Simulation already ran your program with no robot. A test uses that same simulator, but nothing loops unless the test says so.
This test schedules the command that sends the arm straight up. Scheduling only puts it in line, so the motor still has no request.
Then the test runs the scheduler once. One tick. Now the request names the target, and the check passes.
Leave that tick out, and the check fails. It's the most common mistake in this lesson.
The flywheel test fakes the sensor. It sets the speed just inside the tolerance and checks that it counts, then sets it well outside and checks that it doesn't.
Be the teammate. Widen the tolerance, and run the tests.
The far-off speed slides inside the band, and the second check fails. That edit just got caught.
A test checks the request, not the motion. The bench still has to show the arm really gets there.
Put decisions where a test can read them, and let the computer check them every time.

videos.title: Facing One Way, Driving Another
videos.opensFrom: Workshop 4's mechanisms each did one thing; this robot moves in any direction.
videos.handsTo: Thirteen device IDs, which the generator asks for next. Drift sets up calibration, tuning and vision.
videos.gate: Hold a direction and spin the robot; toggle field- and robot-centric.
videos.visuals: New top-down field + swerve robot drawable: four modules at their steer angles with speed arrows that reverse, a front marker and heading arrow, field axes fixed at the blue corner, a driver-forward arrow, a pose readout, and a ghost odometry pose. The controller needs sticks and a left bumper.
lines: A swerve robot can face one way and drive another.
Each corner has a module with two motors. One spins the wheel, and the other points it. You never write the math that coordinates them. Two generated files do that.
Ask for a direction, and all four wheels point that way. Ask for a spin at the same time, and each wheel works out its own angle.
Which way is forward? Robot centric means forward follows the robot's nose. Turn the robot around, and the stick turns with it.
Field centric means forward is down the field, no matter which way the robot faces. For that, it needs a gyro to know its heading.
Try it. Hold a direction, and spin the robot.
On the red side, the driver's forward flips around, so pushing away still drives away from you.
The robot's position is a pose: X down the field, Y across it, and a heading. The origin is the blue corner.
And it stays the blue corner, even when you're on red. Only the driver's forward flips. The field never does.
Odometry tracks the pose by adding up how far each wheel turned, every loop. It only ever adds, so every error stays in.
A wheel slips, someone shoves you, the wheel size is a little off, and the estimate walks away from the truth. Calibration slows that down. Vision corrects it.
Find all thirteen devices on your robot, and write down their IDs. The generator asks for them next.

videos.title: One File From Tuner X
videos.opensFrom: The thirteen IDs from last video.
videos.handsTo: The drivetrain default command, the only setDefaultCommand in the course, reused by Pathfinding's 'let go' beat.
videos.gate: None in the recording; the default-command beat is animated (lane with applyRequest running forever, request card ticking vx 0.0 when the sticks centre).
videos.visuals: Recorded: Devices list, Mechanisms → New Project, four dimension fields, module setup, Encoder Calibration, Verify Steer / Verify Drive, Generate only TunerConstants, VS Code file swap, team number, Simulate Robot Code with AdvantageScope 2D field. Animated: the latched-speed / default-command beat.
lines: Tuner X can measure your drivetrain, test every module, and write one file for you.
Start with thirteen devices on one bus, each with its own ID, and no warnings.
Make a new swerve project, and enter four numbers: front to back, side to side, the wheel's radius, and the drive ratio. The two distance labels are easy to swap, so read them twice.
Then set up each corner. Pick its encoder and its two motors, and hold the wheel straight when it asks. That's the module's zero.
Verify each one. If the wrong corner moves, two IDs are swapped.
Generate only the constants file, and replace yours with it. Then set your team number, and deploy.
You can drive it before the robot's even finished. Run the simulator, push the stick, and watch the pose move on the field.
Three files make the drivetrain. Two come from CTRE. The third, the drive mechanism, is the one your code talks to.

Here's what's different from the arm. A drivetrain's last request is a speed, and you know a request stays on the motor. So teleop gives it a default command that reads the sticks every loop. Let go, and it sends zero.
On blocks, pushing forward lines up all four wheels. On the floor, let go of the sticks, and it stops.
Measure it, generate it, and drive it in simulation before it ever touches the floor.

videos.title: Straight Means Straight
videos.opensFrom: The generator's by-eye wheel zeros.
videos.handsTo: 'A steady curve is a zero, a wander is the gains' — then the carpet, next.
videos.gate: Tilt one module half a degree and drive 6 m down a line: it ends 5 cm off.
videos.visuals: Animated: three 'zeroing' cards on the field drawable (bumper moves forward arrow, perspective flips it, resetPose moves the pose but is greyed 'not exposed'); the half-degree walk. Recorded: straight edge and bevel gears on camera, Encoder Calibration ×4, Generate only TunerConstants, AdvantageScope ModuleStates vs ModuleTargets during stick flicks.
lines: Three different things on a swerve robot get called zeroing, and they reset three different things.
The bumper button resets which way is forward. It doesn't move the robot's position.
The alliance setting flips forward for red. That doesn't touch the position either.
Resetting the pose is what would move it, and nothing calls that yet. For now, the pose is just distance since the robot turned on.
The module zeros came from wheels you held straight by eye. Half a degree off walks the robot five centimeters sideways over six meters.
Try it. Tilt one wheel half a degree, and drive the robot down the line.
So lay a straight edge along both wheels on each side. And check that every bevel gear faces the middle of the robot, or that module zeroes half a turn off.
Run the encoder calibration for each module, generate the constants again, and redeploy.
The steering is a position loop with no gravity, so skip the gravity gain, and start from the static gain. The values it shipped with are usually close.
Plot where each module points against where it was told to point, and flick the stick. Tuned, the two lines sit on top of each other.
A curve that's the same every time is a zero. A wander that comes and goes is the gains.

videos.title: What the Carpet Says
videos.opensFrom: Calibration's 'next, the carpet'.
videos.handsTo: A drivetrain whose numbers match the floor, which Autonomous measures against.
videos.gate: Drag the wheel radius until the tape mark and the odometry mark agree. (Script avoids naming which way the correction goes until SITE-FIXES #5 is settled.)
videos.visuals: Recorded: tape-measure runs, AdvantageScope speed plateau, Voltage Out wall test with stator current, the OpenLoopVoltage → Velocity edit. Animated: tape vs odometry marks with the radius slider; the slip knee on velocity and current traces.
lines: The generator guessed three numbers. The carpet tells you the real ones.
Tune them in order: the wheel radius, then top speed, then slip, and close the speed loop last.
Drive a measured distance, and compare the tape with what odometry says. The ratio between them tells you how far off the radius is.
Try it. Change the radius until the two marks agree.
For top speed, drive flat out, and read where the speed levels off. Use that plateau, not the spike before it.
For slip, push the robot into a wall with Voltage Out, and watch the current climb. Read the top of the climb, right before the wheels break loose.
Then tune the speed loop like any other: the velocity gain, then static, then proportional, with the robot on the ground.
Last, change one word, so the drive asks for a speed instead of a voltage.
And shrink the deadband until the robot twitches at rest, then back off one step.
Measure on the carpet you'll drive on. The file is only as good as the floor you took it from.

videos.title: Fifteen Seconds, No Driver
videos.opensFrom: Raise And Shoot (Coroutines): an autonomous mode that ran the arm with nobody on the sticks.
videos.handsTo: Three end poses scattered by a timer; PathPlanner replaces the timer with a path.
videos.gate: Live Disable key: disable mid-wait and watch the canceled branch send the zero.
videos.visuals: Field drawable with a tape mark; class card (name, start, end) beside the routine's three coroutine lines with a playhead; two request chips (1 m/s forward, all zeros); three end-pose dots.
lines: You've written an autonomous mode once already. Raise and Shoot ran the arm with nobody on the sticks. This one drives the whole robot.
Keep the mode itself thin. It starts the routine, and it ends it. Everything else lives in a command you can test.
The routine is three lines: drive forward at one meter per second, wait, then send a stop.
Pick Leave Start, and enable. The robot leaves its tape mark, and the last line stops it.
Delete that last line, and it never stops. Nothing replaces the request, and autonomous has no default command.
Disable it halfway, and the routine is canceled in the middle of its wait. The last line never runs. That's why the canceled path sends the same stop.
Try it. Disable it whenever you like.
The direction comes from the robot's heading. Rotate it on the tape, and the same routine drives somewhere else.
Test it in layers: on blocks, then on the floor, three times. The three end spots should land within about ten centimeters.
Write down where it ended. Next, a drawn path that knows where it's going replaces the timer.

videos.title: A Path That Knows Where It Ends
videos.opensFrom: Leave Start's three scattered end dots.
videos.handsTo: A drawn path; Pathfinding draws one on the fly.
videos.gate: Shove the robot off the path; the correction pulls it back.
videos.visuals: Recorded: PathPlanner app (Open Robot Project, Robot Config, draw Leave Start 2 m at 45°, the auto with Reset Odometry, the Intake zone), vendordep install. Animated: ghost setpoint leading the robot, a correction arrow, the Intake event starting and stopping at the zone edges, a bumper clipping the hub.
lines: A wait doesn't know where it ends. A path does.
A path is one curve on the field. An auto is a list of steps, and paths are some of them.
First, tell PathPlanner about your robot: its mass, its size, and how hard each wheel can push.
Draw the path from the same tape mark: two meters out, turned forty five degrees. The preview shows the bumpers, so you can see what it'll hit.
Wrap it in an auto, and turn on reset odometry, so the robot starts where the path does.
In code, the drive mechanism tells the library four things: where the robot is, how to reset that, how fast it's moving, and how to drive it.
One autonomous mode registers the named commands, builds the drop down of autos, and reads the choice when the match starts.
On the field, the plan moves ahead, and the robot follows it. When it drifts, a correction pulls it back.
Try it. Shove the robot off the path.
Paths can carry events. In the intake zone, the intake runs, and it stops when the robot leaves.
Three runs of the path land closer together than three runs of the timer. That's the point.

videos.title: Seeing the Field
videos.opensFrom: Autos trust the pose, and the pose drifts (How Swerve Works).
videos.handsTo: The camera's name; the code that feeds sightings into the pose is next.
videos.gate: Drag the camera's mount angle until the cloud of solved poses is tight.
videos.visuals: Animated: odometry ghost peeling away vs a fixed-size cloud of tag sightings; a tag's ID and field spot, corners solved back to a pose; square-on vs angled tag and the error cloud. Recorded: Limelight web UI (field map, AprilTag pipeline, exposure, offsets, ChArUco, name), tag check at 1 m. Verify UI labels on the device.
lines: Your autos trust the robot's pose, and every skid goes into it and stays there.
Odometry drifts further the longer you drive. A camera that sees a tag gives an answer that doesn't drift. It's noisy, but the error doesn't grow.
An AprilTag has an ID and a known spot on the field. From its four corners, the camera works backwards to where the robot must be.
Those sightings come now and then, and they're noisy, so they don't replace odometry. The next lesson blends the two.
Mount the camera where it sees the scoring tags while you're scoring, and give it its own breaker.
Never mount it level and square to a tag. Head on, small errors smear the answer. At an angle, the answer tightens up.
Try it. Move the camera until the cloud of answers is tight.
In the camera's web page, load the field map, pick the AprilTag pipeline, and turn the exposure down.
Enter where the camera sits on the robot, calibrate it with the ChArUco board, and give it a name.
Hold a tag a meter away. You should see its ID, the right distance, and a pose that holds steady.
Write down the camera's name. Next, the code feeds these sightings into the pose.

videos.title: Blending, Not Replacing
videos.opensFrom: The camera's name from last video.
videos.handsTo: A pose that stays honest, which Drive to Point drives to.
videos.gate: Cover the camera, push the robot, uncover: the estimate walks home. Sliders for distance and tag count.
videos.visuals: Field drawable with a ghost estimate pulled toward sightings; error circles sized by distance and tag count; rejected dots greying out; a two-clock strip (camera frames vs robot loops) for the frame queue; a rewind-fold-replay of the pose trail. Recorded: ~8 s vendordep install.
lines: The camera can see a tag and work out where the robot is. Now the robot has to listen.
Install the Limelight library from its vendor file. The address is pinned to the WPILib alpha, so copy it exactly.
There are two ways to solve a pose. One works out the heading from the tags. The other borrows the robot's own heading, and that's the one to trust with a single tag.
So every loop, the robot sends its heading to the camera first.
The camera and the robot run on different clocks. Reading the frame queue takes exactly the frames that arrived, no more and no fewer.
Some sightings get thrown out: anything the library flags, and anything more than four meters away.
The rest get weighed. Far away, the error circle grows. A second tag shrinks it to a quarter.
Each picture was taken a moment ago. The estimator rewinds to that moment, folds the sighting in, and replays forward to now.
Try it. Cover the camera, push the robot, then uncover it.
It doesn't jump. The estimate walks back over about a second, and faster when the sighting is good.
Blend the camera into the pose. Don't replace the pose with the camera.

videos.title: Speed From Distance
videos.opensFrom: Every meter so far, a person drove; the pose is now honest (Vision).
videos.handsTo: Bolts, then creeps short: Profiled Drive to Point plans the trip instead.
videos.gate: Drag the goal pose and hold A.
videos.visuals: Field drawable; goal ghost at (3, 2, 180°); three error arrows (X, Y, heading); speed arrow pinned to the 4.54 m/s ring; heading dial showing the ±180° wrap; a module-bar strip comparing the zero stop with Idle.
lines: Hold a button, and the robot drives itself to a spot on the field.
Every meter so far, a person drove. Now the robot uses its own pose.
The goal is a pose too: three meters, two meters, facing the other way.
The command is the same loop you already know. Start, run every loop, check if it's done, and stop on the way out.
Three controllers run at once: one for X, one for Y, and one for heading. Each one turns its error into a speed.
Heading needs one extra line. Otherwise, turning from a hundred seventy nine degrees to minus a hundred seventy nine goes the long way around.
Three meters out, with a gain of ten, it asks for thirty meters per second. The robot can't do that, so it runs flat out.
Try it. Drag the goal somewhere else, and hold the button.
Close to the goal, the error is small, so the speed is small, and it creeps up short. That's the falls short shape from tuning.
Let go, and the command ends with a zero speed request. Sending idle instead would leave every wheel on its last speed.
Speed from distance gets you there, badly. Next, plan the trip.

videos.title: Plan the Trip
videos.opensFrom: Last video's flat-out bolt and crawl.
videos.handsTo: A command with an ending: a step that can go in a sequence.
videos.gate: Shove the robot mid-trip; flip the correction gain between 10 and 3.
videos.visuals: Field drawable with a ghost robot on the plan; the Motion Magic velocity plot re-axised in meters (2.5 m/s cruise, 3.0 m/s² ramp), folding to a triangle under 2.1 m; a big feedforward arrow and a small correction arrow; the plan's clock.
lines: Plan the whole trip before the robot moves, then follow the plan.
Last time, it asked for thirty meters per second, then crawled the last stretch.
You've seen this shape on the arm: speed up, cruise, slow down. Now it's in meters.
On a trip under about two meters, there's no room to cruise, so the plan is a triangle.
When you press the button, the plan starts from where the robot is, and how fast it's already moving.
Every loop, the clock moves forward, and the plan says where the robot should be, and how fast it should go.
The plan's speed does most of the driving. A small correction pulls the robot toward where it should be.
Try it. Shove the robot, and flip the correction gain between ten and three.
At ten, a few centimeters of drift turn into meters per second. That's the buzz shape. Three is calm.
The command ends when the plan's clock runs out, even if the robot is a little short. That ending is what makes it a step.
A command with an ending can go in a list, after anything else.

videos.title: Starting From Anywhere
videos.opensFrom: PathPlanner's drawn path starts where you drew it.
videos.handsTo: The last few centimeters belong to a purpose-built command (Drive to Tag).
videos.gate: Widen the margin slider, or wall off the shortest route, and watch it re-plan.
videos.visuals: Animated: 0.3 m grid with blocked cells, the robot's centre dot threading open cells while the bumper clears, a route redrawing while driving and freezing at 2 m, the drive default lane taking over on release. Recorded: PathPlanner Navigation Grid page; AdvantageScope 2D field trail around the hub.
lines: A drawn path starts where you drew it. Pathfinding starts wherever the robot is.
PathPlanner splits the field into squares about thirty centimeters across, and marks the ones you can't drive through.
The margin is your bumper. The center of the robot threads through open squares, so the bumpers clear the walls.
It searches for a route, then keeps refining it while the robot drives, until it's close to the goal.
In code, it's two lines: set up the pathfinder once, then ask for a pose with speed limits.
Hold the button, and the robot routes around the hub to its goal.
Let go halfway. A canceled path sends no stop, but the drive's default command takes over and sends zero.
Try it. Widen the margin, or wall off the shortest way.
If it clips the hub, the margin's too small, or the robot's size is wrong in the settings.
Pathfinding crosses the field. The last few centimeters belong to a command built for them.

videos.title: Every Way Out Stops
videos.opensFrom: Drive to Point needed a field pose; this needs only the tag.
videos.handsTo: End of the course's code.
videos.gate: Cover the camera mid-approach: it stops, waits up to a second, and gives up stopped.
videos.visuals: Field drawable with the tag's own axes; three profiled controllers as small trapezoids; the coroutine loop with read / drive / yield lit in turn; three exit doors (arrive, give up, canceled), each sending a stop. Page code is ground truth (7-InlineCommands is behind).
lines: Hold a button, and the robot drives to a meter in front of a tag, using nothing but the camera.
Drive to point needed a pose on the field. This one only needs the tag.
The camera reports the robot's position in the tag's own frame. We pick our tag's ID, and ignore the rest.
Three profiled controllers do the driving: one for distance, one for sideways, and one to square up.
Facing the tag means a half turn in its frame, because the tag faces out toward the robot.
It's one loop: read the tag, drive, yield, and repeat. The same shape you wrote in Coroutines.
If the tag disappears, it stops, waits up to a second for it to come back, and gives up stopped.
When the tag comes back, the profiles start fresh from where the robot is, so it doesn't lurch.
Three ways out: it arrives, it gives up, or it's canceled. Every one sends a stop on the way out.
One loop, and a stop on every way out.
